items.title: Buying data, inheriting liability: Cyber and data due diligence in Indian M&A
items.summary: When a company acquires a business, it acquires that business's data, along with any failure in how that data was collected, secured or shared. That exposure is no longer theoretical. IBM's 2026 study put the average cost of a data breach in India at ₹25.5 crore ( IBM India, 2026 ). From May 13, 2027, the substantive provisions of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP Act) will add penalties of up to ₹250 crore. My argument is that data must be diligenced as a liability, not only valued as an asset. Transactions signed today will close, or be integrated, under the new regime. Question: Why has data become a core diligence issue in Indian transactions now? Answer: Three developments have converged. First, the DPDP Act's substantive obligations, including security safeguards and breach intimation, are scheduled to take effect on May 13, 2027 ( Mondaq, Aug 2026 ), giving a target's compliance gaps a statutory price. The party passed the resolution at a meeting of its Members of Parliament chaired by DMK president MK Stalin. The party has 22 MPs in the Lok Sabha and eight in the Rajya Sabha. The draft Bill, released by the Union government on Friday, November 27, addresses most of the key demands raised by the DMK. The proposed changes come amid sustained opposition from several southern states, which have argued that delimitation based on population could penalise states that have successfully implemented family-planning measures and brought down population growth. items.title: Is the Tribunal Reforms Act, 2026 calling for a seventh round of Madras Bar Association litigation?
items.summary: It is beyond doubt that tribunals today decide some of the most important disputes in India, covering areas such as taxation, insolvency, company law, service matters and telecommunications. In many of these disputes, the government is itself a party. This makes one question central to every round of the Madras Bar Association’s (MBA) litigation over the last 15 years: who gets to choose the people who decide these disputes and should the government have the final say in it? The Tribunal Reforms Act, 2026 , which came into force on August 25, 2026, appears to address the Supreme Court of India’s concerns. It establishes the National Tribunals Commission (NTC), as directed by the Court, and follows its directions on tenure and the number of candidates to be recommended for each post. However, it removes one safety-net that the Supreme Court has sought since 1987 and expressly required since 2010: a Supreme Court judge nominated by the Chief Justice of India (CJI) as the chairperson of the selection committees for most tribunals. items.title: Delhi High Court bars Bajaj Finance from using AI-facial recognition cameras to profile visitors without consent
items.summary: The Delhi High Court on Friday restrained Bajaj Finance, Bajaj Finance Securities and Bajaj Housing Finance from using artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled facial recognition cameras at its branches and authorised dealer stores to allegedly capture and profile customers and others who visited their offices/ dealerships. Justice Jasmeet Singh said that the company can continue to use the technology for Know Your Customer (KYC) verification but cannot use the tech to capture images of any and every person walking into their store, without their consent. The Court added that Bajaj cannot share the data collected through these cameras with any other entity. “For the said reasons, the respondent Nos. 2 to 4 [Bajaj Finance, Bajaj Finance Securities and Bajaj Housing Finance], their agents, employees, representatives and any persons acting on their behalf are restrained from collecting and using the information collected by way of these facial recognition cameras for purpose other than KYC. Furthermore, the respondent Nos. 2 to 4 are specifically restrained from sharing the said data with any other entity, including group entities,” the Court ordered.
